## Original note content

---
title: "Chapter 1: The UK Tax System and Its Administration"
abstract: |
  This chapter introduces the overall structure and purpose of the United Kingdom
  tax system within the ACCA TX-UK syllabus. It explains why taxation exists,
  distinguishes direct and indirect taxation, identifies the main capital and
  revenue taxes, and summarises the legal and administrative framework in which
  HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) operates. The chapter also outlines
  self-assessment, filing and payment deadlines, compliance activity, and the
  ethical responsibilities of tax advisers. The aim is to provide a professional,
  exam-focused foundation for later computational and advisory topics.
---

# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

This study paper provides a structured overview of the UK tax system for ACCA
TX-UK. It is written in a concise reference style so that key definitions,
comparisons, and administrative rules can be revised quickly.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
## Chapter Focus

- Purpose of taxation in a modern economy
- Direct and indirect taxation
- Capital and revenue taxes
- Revenue law, practice, and HMRC guidance
- Self-assessment and tax administration
- Ethics, avoidance, and evasion
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
## Revision Route

- Start with [purpose of taxation](#sec-purpose-taxation)
- Compare [direct and indirect taxes](#sec-direct-indirect)
- Learn the [main UK taxes](#sec-main-taxes)
- Review [sources of revenue law](#sec-revenue-law)
- Finish with [ethics and professional conduct](#sec-ethics)
:::
:::

# The UK Tax System and Its Administration {#sec-uk-tax-system}

## The Overall Function and Purpose of Taxation {#sec-purpose-taxation}

### Purpose of Taxation {#sec-tax-purpose}

Taxation serves both **economic** and **social** objectives.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
#### Economic Purpose

- Funds public expenditure and public services
- Influences inflation, employment, and trade activity
- Encourages or discourages particular behaviour
- Supports wider fiscal policy goals
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
#### Social Purpose

- Contributes to redistribution of wealth
- Supports social justice objectives
- Shapes fairness through tax burden design
- Can target support to specific groups
:::
:::

The current UK tax system may encourage:

- Individual saving through tax-advantaged products such as Individual savings accounts (ISAs)
- Charitable giving through reliefs such as Gift Aid
- Entrepreneurship and investment through targeted reliefs

The current UK tax system may discourage:

- Motoring through fuel duties
- Smoking and alcohol consumption through excise duties
- Environmental damage

# The scope of income tax

## Basis of assessment

Individuals are assessed to income tax on their income arising in a **tax year**. 

The UK tax year runs from 6 April to 5 April the following year.

- Current Tax Year (2026/27): Began on 6 April 2026 and will end on 5 April 2027.
- Previous Tax Year (2025/26): Ran from 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026.

## Assessable persons

- All individuals, including children, are chargeable to income tax.
- Both spouses within a married couple and both partners in a civil partnership are treated as separate individuals for the purposes of income tax.

The tax residency status of an individual determines how much income is assessed to UK tax.  
All persons resident for tax purposes in the UK are assessed to UK tax on their worldwide income.

## Personal allowance 

Every taxpayer is entitled to a personal allowance (PA). 

- The PA is an amount of tax-free income that every taxpayer is entitled to each tax year. 
- The amount is reduced, potentially to £Nil, for high income individuals.

## Married couples and civil partners 

There are special rules governing the allocation of income between spouses where assets are jointly owned: 

Generally, income generated from assets jointly owned is split 50:50 between spouses regardless of the actual percentage ownership.

**Election available:** Where jointly owned assets are held other than in a 50:50 ratio, an election can be made to HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) for the income  to be taxed on the individual spouses according to their actual percentage  ownership.  

Civil partners are treated in the same way as married couples.

# Property income - basis of assessment for individuals or partnerships 

## Basis of assessment (Cash Basis)

The amount assessable for a tax year is usually the net profit arising from the letting of all properties owned by the landlord in the tax year ending on **5 April**.

Property income can be assessed using the cash basis, or the accruals basis. However, the **cash basis is the default basis** for an individual with property income.

> The cash basis is the default basis for non-corporate bodies with property income, therefore in exam questions involving property income for **individuals or partnerships**, it should be assumed that the cash basis is used, unless a question specifically states otherwise.

The rental income and related expenses are assessable/deductible on a received/paid basis. Accordingly, the period to which the income/expense relates is irrelevant. 

## Allowable deductions 

The types of allowable expenses for property income are generally the same as those allowable under the normal rules for the assessment of trading income. 

The main rules are as follows: 

- The general rule is that to be allowable, the expenses must have been incurred wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the property business.   
  This covers items such as:

    - Insurance
    - Agents' fees and other management expenses 
    - Repairs
    - interest on a loan to acquire or improve a **let non-residential property**.

> there are special rules which apply to the **financing costs** of a let **residential property**.

**Non-residential property**

- For **non-residential property** (e.g., offices, shops, warehouses), interest on loans taken out to buy or improve the property is treated as a straightforward **deductible expense**.  
- This means it can be offset directly against rental income when calculating taxable property profits.

**Residential property**

- For **residential property**, the rules are different.  
- Since April 2020, landlords cannot deduct finance costs (like mortgage interest) in full from rental income.  
- Instead, they receive a **basic rate tax reduction (20%)** on those costs.

# The scope of employment income

## Employment or self-employment

The distinction between employment and self-employment is fundamental: 

```{=typst}
#table(
  columns: (1fr, 1fr),
  stroke: none,
  inset: 0pt,
  [An employee is taxable under the employment income provisions],
  [A self-employed person is assessed on the profits derived from a trade, profession or vocation, under the trading income provisions.]
)
```
---

However, even in the absence of a written contract of service any of the following matters would corroborate the existence of such a contract, and, therefore, employment:

- Mutuality of obligations: an obligation by the employer to offer work and an obligation by the employee to undertake the work offered. An employee would not normally be in a position to decline work when offered.
- Control: the employer controls the manner and method of the work 
- Benefits: the individual is entitled to benefits normally provided to employees such as sick pay and holiday pay.
- Basis of payment: the individual is committed to work a specified number of hours at certain fixed times, and is paid by the hour, week or month. 
- Length of engagement: the engagement is for a long period of time. 
- Equipment: equipment is not provided by the individual 
- Personal service: the individual is obliged to work personally and exclusively for the employer, and cannot hire any helpers. 
- Part and parcel of organisation: the work performed by the individual is an integral part of the business of the employer, and not merely an accessory to it. 
- Financial risk: the economic reality of self-employment is missing namely the financial risk arising from not being paid an agreed, regular amount. 
- Sound management: the individual cannot profit from sound management. 

### Tax advantages of self-employment 

There are some tax advantages to an individual being classed as self-employed rather than employed: 

- National insurance: For the contracting organisation there is no employers’ NIC to be paid. For the self-employed individual lower NIC rates apply.
- PAYE: Income tax and the individual’s NIC do not have to be collected under PAYE. Income tax and NIC are therefore paid later under self assessment.
- Expenses: There are less strict rules with regard to the deductibility of expenses.

title: "Chapter 6: Pensions"
abstract: |
     explain and compute the relief given for contributions to personal pension schemes, and to occupational pension schemes. 
---

# Types of registered pension schemes (Occupational and Personal)

An individual can set up an investment of funds to provide an income during retirement in a tax efficient way by making payments into a *registered* pension scheme.

A pension scheme is a *savings plan* for retirement that enjoys special tax privileges, but only if the scheme is registered with HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC).

The conditions that a pension scheme must satisfy to be registered with HMRC are excluded from the TX examination. Therefore, the exam will not refer to the scheme being a “registered” pension scheme as such, and you can assume that a pension scheme in the exam will be “registered”.  

Investing in a pension scheme is a *long term investment* and is very tax efficient for the following reasons:

- The individual obtains tax relief on the contributions made into the scheme. 
- Where an employer contributes into the scheme, tax relief for the employer contributions is available *without there being a taxable benefit* for the employee. 
- Pension scheme funds grow tax-free as the scheme is exempt from income tax and capital gains tax. 
- Some funds can be withdrawn as a tax-free lump sum on retirement. This amount is not examinable. 

The two main types of pension scheme available are: 

- **Occupational** pension schemes 
- **Personal** pension schemes.

A self-employed or unemployed individual *can only set up a personal pension scheme*. 

An employed individual may: 

- Join an occupational pension scheme provided by the employer (the employee may be automatically enrolled depending on the size of the employer), or 
- Choose not to join the employer’s scheme and set up a personal pension scheme, or 
- Contribute into both the employer’s occupational scheme and set up a personal pension scheme. 


## Automatic enrolment in an employer-sponsored pension scheme 

There is a legal duty for employers to provide a pension scheme to the majority of employees under *automatic enrolment*. The scheme provided can be an occupational or a personal pension scheme.

## Occupational pension schemes 

An occupational pension scheme is a scheme set up by a specific employer for the benefit of its employees.

The employer may use an **insurance company** to provide and run a pension scheme for employees, or it may set up its own **self-administered pension fund**. 

Contributions into an occupational scheme may be made by both the employer and the employee.

--- # Income from self-employment ## Basis of assessment for self-employment The profits of an unincorporated trader arising from a trade, profession or vocation are taxed as trading income. Individuals with an unincorporated business are usually referred to as 'self-employed' or 'sole traders'. For tax years up to *2022/23 profits* of an ongoing business were taxed on a ***current year basis (CYB)***, i.e. the trading income taxed in a particular tax year were the profits of the 12-month accounting period ending in that tax year. This basis of assessment is ***no longer examinable***. ### Tax year 2023/24: Transitional year To move from one system to the other, businesses with accounting dates not aligned to 31 March/5 April had to bring extra months of profit into charge. These extra profits are called transition profits. For the tax year 2023/24 transitional rules applied. These are special rules for taxing the profits of any business where the accounting period is **not aligned with the tax year**, i.e. any business that did not have an accounting period ending on 5 April or 31 March. Additional transition profits may have arisen that will automatically be spread over **five years**. There was also an option to ***override*** the five year spreading of transition profits and tax the full amount in 2023/24. You are only required to have an awareness of *basis period* reform and that transition profits will be taxed in the future. The **calculation** of transition profits and the election to override the five year spreading **are not examinable** in the TX exam. Furthermore, the **interaction** between transition profits and the annual allowance, the child benefit tax charge and the restriction on income tax reliefs set against other income **are not examinable**. In the TX examination, you may be given the amount of transition profits and be required to tax these in any of the tax years 2025/26 to 2027/28: - One fifth of the transition profits will be taxed in each of these years. - The transition profits are included as a separate amount of non-savings income in the income tax computation. - The transition profits may impact on the availability of the personal allowance. ### Ta

title: "Chapter 9: Partnerships"
abstract: |
    explain and compute how a partnership is assessed to tax.

![](20260731082100.png)

# Basis of Assessment

## Introduction

A partnership is a body of persons carrying on business together with a view to profit. 


- Each partner is taxed **individually**, despite the partnership being a single trading entity, with its own accounts.
- Each partner is taxed based on their *allocated share* of the partnership profits as if the partner were a sole trader making that amount of profit.
- To determine a partner’s taxable profits: 
    
    - Firstly, the trading profits of the partnership are calculated for tax purposes as for a sole trader, on the ***cash basis by default or the accruals basis by election*** (Chapter 7).
    - Secondly, deduct the capital allowances of the partnership if using the accruals basis or claiming capital allowances on cars under the cash basis (Chapter 8). 
    - Thirdly, the taxable trading profits of the partnership are allocated to the individual partners 
    - Finally, each of the partners are taxed on their allocation of the taxable profits on a tax year basis. Therefore, if the partnership accounts are not prepared to a 31 March/5 April year end the partners’ allocated profits will need to be ***time apportioned*** to calculate the taxable trading income for the tax year. 

## The allocation of profits and losses

### The computation of partnership profits and losses

The principles of computation of a partnership’s trading profits for tax purposes are the same as those for a sole trader. 

Partners’ salaries and interest on capital ***are not deductible expenses for tax purposes***, since these are merely an allocation of profit.                    
As for sole traders, the cash basis will be used for partnerships by default, but the accruals basis is available by election. ***Flat rate expenses*** are also available, as for a sole trader.  


### The allocation of the profit or loss

The taxable trading profit or loss is allocated (divided) between the partners according to their *profit sharing arrangements* for that period of account. 

Partners may be entitled by the partnership agreement to ‘salaries’ (a fixed allocation of profit) and ‘interest on capital’. 

The balance of profits remaining after the allocation of any ‘salaries’ or interest is allocated in the ***profit sharing ratio (PSR)***.

--- # Personal tax administration The collection of income tax Employees have their income tax and national insurance contribution (NIC) liabilities on their employment income, and in some cases on small amounts of other income, collected at source through the *PAYE system*. **Self-assessment** is the system for the collection of tax, which is **not deducted through the PAYE system**. Therefore, employees with more complicated tax affairs and other taxpayers (e.g. the self-employed) will normally be required to submit details of their taxable income and gains annually in a tax return, so that their tax liability can be calculated and collected through the **self-assessment system**. ## Self-assessment Under the self-assessment system for individuals, taxpayers are responsible for providing the information to calculate the tax liability on the income tax return: - The taxpayer will be sent a notice to complete a self-assessment tax return annually. A return must be completed and filed – either on paper or online. - Different deadlines exist for filing paper and electronic (online) returns. - The tax return covers income tax and class 4 NICs and capital gains tax (CGT) liabilities for the tax year. - **Payment** of the tax must be made by 31 January following the end of the tax year to which it relates. - Interim payments on account in respect of income tax and class 4 NIC may be required on 31 January in the tax year and 31 July following the tax year for certain taxpayers. ### Return – filing deadline The deadline f

--- ![](20260811173745.png) Associated companies were defined in Chapter 13. In group questions in the TX examination it is often necessary to determine the number of associates, or to state which companies are associated and potentially why. # Group relief group Group loss relief is available to members of a 75% group relief group. Losses of one member of the group can be surrendered to other group companies, to utilise against their own taxable total profits. ## Introduction ### Definition of a 75% group relief group Two companies are members of a 75% group relief group where one company is the 75% subsidiary of the other, or both companies are 75% subsidiaries of a third company. A company (the parent company) has a 75% subsidiary if it owns, directly or indirectly, at least 75% of its ordinary share capital, and it has the right to 75% or more of its distributable profits, and it has the right to 75% or more of its net assets on a winding up. For sub-subsidiaries to be in a group, the parent company must have an effective interest in the sub-subsidiary of at least 75%. Groups can be created through companies resident overseas. However, for the purposes of the TX examination, the companies actually claiming/surrendering group relief must be resident in the UK. Companies can be in more than one loss relief group. ### Implications of being in a group relief group Where a group of companies form a group relief group: - Losses of one group company may be surrendered to other companies in the group. - The recipient company can then relieve the losses against its own taxable total profits. A loss may be surrendered by any member company to any other member of the same group, provided they are UK resident. ## Mechanics of group relief - Companies which form part of the same group relief group can transfer losses between each other. - The surrendering company is the company that surrenders its loss. - The claimant company is the company to which the loss is surrendered. - The losses which may be surrendered are: - trading losses - current period - brought forward trading losses to the extent that they cannot be used against the surrendering company’s own total profits - unrelieved QCDs - unrelieved property busi

--- ![](20260812133220.png) # The self-assessment system for companies As for individuals, self-assessment applies for corporate taxpayers. Responsibility rests with the company to: - calculate its own corporation tax liability for each accounting period - submit a self-assessment corporation tax return within 12 months after the end of the period of account - pay any corporation tax due within nine months and one day after the end of the accounting period. Given the timing of the due date for payment of tax, in practice, many companies will aim to complete the self-assessment tax return prior to the nine month deadline for paying the corporation tax. ***The self-assessment tax return*** The self-assessment tax return must be submitted by the later of: - 12 months after the end of the period of account, and - three months after the issue of the notice to file a return. ***The return must:*** - contain all information required to calculate the company’s taxable total profits - include a self-assessment of the amount of corporation tax payable for that accounting period - be submitted online. A company has to submit a copy of its financial accounts together with the self-assessment tax return. All companies must file self-assessment returns and copies of accounts electronically using **'Inline eXtensible Business Reporting Language' (iXBRL).** iXBRL is the global standard for exchanging business information in an electronic format and tags the accounts so they can be read by a computer. HMRC provide free online filing software applications for companies with straightforward tax affairs that automatically produces and submits a self-assessment return with accounts and computations in the required iXBRL format, as well as calculating the tax liability. Original notes: [C17_CGT.QMD](../C17_CGT.QMD) Related: [[C18_CGT_Special]], [[C19_CGT_SH]], [[C20_CGT_Relief]], [[C21_CG_Corp]] ## Original note content --- title: "Chapter 17: Computation of gains and tax payable" abstract: | 1. describe the scope of capital gains tax.

--- ![](20260813172112.png) # Scope of capital gains tax Capital gains tax (CGT) is charged on gains arising on chargeable persons making chargeable disposals of chargeable assets. ## Chargeable persons Chargeable persons include individuals and companies. In these CGT chapters we are concerned with disposals by individuals. - Individuals who are UK resident in the tax year in which the disposal takes place are subject to capital gains tax on their gains. - UK resident individuals are subject to UK CGT on all disposals of chargeable assets, regardless of where in the world the assets are situated. - Non-UK residents only pay UK CGT on the disposal of interests in UK land. However, this is not examinable. ::::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%" style="border-right: 2px solid #2c3e50; padding-right: 20px;"} ## Chargeable assets All forms of capital assets, wherever situated, are **chargeable assets**. **Common examples include:** - Freehold land and buildings - Goodwill - Unquoted shares - Quoted shares - Certain types of chattels – Chapter 18 > **Note:** Chattels are tangible movable assets (e.g. furniture, plant and machinery). ::: ::: {.column width="50%" style="padding-left: 20px;"} ## Exempt assets **Exempt assets include:** - Motor vehicles (including vintage cars) - Main residence - Cash - Certain types of chattels – Chapter 18 - Investments held within an ISA - Qualifying corporate bonds (QCBs) - Gilt‑edged securities - NS&I certificates - Foreign currency for private use - Receivables - Trading inventory - Prizes and betting winnings - Decorations for valour (unless purchased) ::: ::::: ## Calculation of capital gain/loss on individual disposals An individual is subject to CGT on the total taxable gains arising on the disposal of all assets in a tax year. The following steps are carried out to compute the capital gains tax payable by an individual for a tax year: | Step | Description | |------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------| | 1 | Calculate the chargeable gain/allowable loss arising on the disposal of each chargeable asset separately | | 2 | Calculate th

# C18 — Special capital gains cases Special rules for capital gains, including transactions or assets requiring treatment different from the standard disposal computation. Original notes: [C18_CGT_Special.qmd](../C18_CGT_Special.qmd) Related: [[C17_CGT]], [[C19_CGT_SH]], [[C20_CGT_Relief]] ## Original note content --- title: "Chapter 18: Computation of gains: Special rules" abstract: | 1. understand the treatment of transfers between spouses or between a couple in a civil partnership.

Transfers between spouses or civil partners Where an asset is transferred between spouses or civil partners: • no gain or loss arises on the transfer • any actual proceeds are ignored • the transferor is deemed to dispose of the asset at its acquisition cost • the deemed proceeds of the transferor are treated as the deemed acquisition cost of the transferee (i.e. the recipient spouse acquires the asset at its original acquisition cost). # Transfers between spouses or civil partners Where an asset is transferred between spouses or civil partners: - no gain or loss arises on the transfer - any actual proceeds are ignored - the transferor is deemed to dispose of the asset at its acquisition cost - the deemed proceeds of the transferor are treated as the deemed acquisition cost of the transferee (i.e. the recipient spouse acquires the asset at its original acquisition cost). #### Example 1: Transfers between spouses and civil partners David purchased some jewellery in August 2005 for £50,000. In July 2025 he gave it to his wife Victoria when it was worth £200,000. Calculate the deemed sale proceeds of David’s disposal and state Victoria’s deemed acquisition cost. **Solution** David is **deemed** to have transferred the asset at its acquisition cost so that no gain or loss arises on the transfer. The deemed proceeds are therefore £50,000 and Victoria’s deemed acquisition cost is the same as David’s deemed proceeds (i.e. £50,000). ***Subsequent disposal by transferee*** On a subsequent disposal of the transferred asset by the transferee, the deemed acquisition cost (often referred to as the base cost of the asset) is the original acquisition cost to t

# C19 — Capital gains on shares Capital-gains treatment of share disposals, reorganisations, and share-specific computational issues. Original notes: [C19_CGT_SH.qmd](../C19_CGT_SH.qmd) Related: [[C17_CGT]], [[C18_CGT_Special]], [[C20_CGT_Relief]], [[C21_CG_Corp]] ## Original note content --- title: "Chapter 19: CGT: Shares and securities for individuals" abstract: | 1. recognise the value of quoted shares where they are disposed of by way of a gift.

--- # Government securities and qualifying corporate bonds All shares and securities disposed of by an individual are subject to capital gains tax except for the following, which are exempt: - listed government securities (gilt-edged securities or gilts) - qualifying corporate bonds (e.g. company loan notes) - shares held in an Individual Savings Account (ISA). ***Definition of a qualifying corporate bond*** A qualifying corporate bond (QCB) is one that: (a) represents a normal commercial loan (b) is expressed in sterling and has no provision for either conversion into, or redemption in, any other currency, and (c) was issued after ***13 March 1984*** or was acquired by the disposer after that date (whenever it was issued). # Valuation of quoted shares On a sale of shares between unconnected parties, the actual proceeds are used in the capital gains computation. However, it is necessary to identify the market value of quoted shares when shares are either: - gifted - transferred to a connected party. For capital gains tax purposes, their market value is determined by taking the **mid-price (i.e. average)** of the prices quoted in the Stock Exchange Daily Official List on the disposal date. #### Example 1: Valuation of quoted shares The shares in Panda plc are quoted in the Stock Exchange Daily OfficialList at 230p - 270p. If a disposal of Panda plc shares were made on that day to ***aconnected party***, what would their value be for CGT purposes? **Solution** The value of Panda plc shares is 250p, being the: Average of the two quoted prices = (270p + 230p) x 1/2 = 250p #### Example 2: Valuation of quoted shares The shares in Sawyer plc are quoted in the Stock Exchange Daily Official List at 460p – 540p. If a **gift** of Sawyer plc shares were made on that day, what would their value be for CGT purposes? **Solution** ## Identification rules It is necessary to have identification (or matching) rules to determine ***which*** shares have been disposed of as: - Shares and securities that are boug

The main reliefs available to individuals are as follows: ![](20260816074541.png) # Private residence relief (PRR) PRR applies when an individual disposes of: - a dwelling house (including normally up to half a hectare of adjoining land) - which has at some time during their ownership been their only or main private residence. The relief applies where the main residence has been occupied for either the whole or part of the period of ownership. ![](20260816075843.png) ## Calculating the relief Where there has been a period of absence from the main residence the procedure is: 1. Calculate the gain on the disposal of the property. 2. Compute the total period of ownership. 3. Calculate the periods of occupation (covered below). 4. Calculate the PRR as follows: Gain × (Periods of occupation/Total period of ownership) 5. Deduct the PRR from the gain on the property. ***Periods of occupation*** The period of occupation includes periods of **both actual occupation and deemed occupation**. Periods of deemed occupation are: A. the ***last nine months*** of ownership (always exempt, unconditionally as long as the dwelling has been the main residence at some point) B. up to **three years** of absence for any reason C. any period spent living **overseas** due to employment D. up to four years of absence as a result of working elsewhere in the UK (employed or self-employed). :::{.callout-note} The absences in (b) to (d) must be preceded and *followed by a period of actual occupation*. The condition to reoccupy the property after the period of absence does not need to be satisfied for (c) and (d) where an employer requires the individual to work elsewhere immediately, thus making it impossible to resume occupation. Original notes: [C21_CG_Corp.qmd](../C21_CG_Corp.qmd) Related: [[C13_Corp_TX]], [[C15_Groups]], [[C17_CGT]], [[C20_CGT_Relief]] ## Original note content --- title: "Chapter 21: Chargeable gains for companies" abstract: | 1. compute and explain the treatment of chargeable gains .

It is important to remember that companies pay **corporation tax** on **chargeable gains**, not capital gains tax. ## Calculation of total net chargeable gains for a company The following steps should be completed: 1. Calculate the chargeable gain/allowable loss arising on the disposal of each chargeable asset separately. 2. # C22 — Inheritance tax Inheritance-tax framework, transfers, exemptions, reliefs, taxable estates, and the timing of liabilities. Original notes: [C22_Inherit.qmd](../C22_Inherit.qmd) Related: [[C01_TX_SYS]], [[C10_TL_IND]], [[C17_CGT]], [[C20_CGT_Relief]] ## Original note content --- title: "Chapter 22: Inheritance tax" abstract: | 1. identify the persons chargeable.
2. understand and apply the meaning of transfer of value, chargeable transfer and potentially exempt transfer.
3. demonstrate the diminution in value principle.
4. demonstrate the seven year accumulation principle taking into account changes in the level of the nil rate band.
5. understand the tax implications of lifetime transfers and compute the relevant liabilities.
6. understand and compute the tax liability on a death estate.

--- > Most inheritance tax (IHT) is collected on the death of an individual based on the value of the individual’s death estate. However, if IHT only applied on death, it would be an easy tax to avoid by giving away assets immediately before death. Therefore, there are IHT implications arising on some lifetime gifts as well as on death. # The charge to inheritance tax (IHT) Inheritance tax is charged on: - a transfer of value - of chargeable property - by a chargeable person. A charge to inheritance tax (IHT) arises: - on the death of an individual - on lifetime gifts to individuals when the donor dies within seven years of the date of a gift - on lifetime gifts into trusts which are taxed at the date of the gift. The donor is the person who makes the transfer of the asset, and the recipient is known as the donee. ***Transfer of value*** A transfer of value is a gift of any asset which results in a reduction in the value of the donor’s estate. To be treated as a transfer of value the transfer must be a ***‘gratuitous disposition’***. This basically means a gift. A bad business deal will therefore **not be liable** to inheritance tax, even though there is a fall in value of the estate, as it was not the donor’s intention to give anything away. To calculate the transfer of value for IHT purposes, the loss to donor principle is used (also referred to as the diminution in value concept). The loss to the donor is the difference between the va

--- ![](20260820151429.png) VAT is: - an indirect tax on consumer spending - charged on most goods and services supplied within the UK - suffered by the final consumer, and - collected by businesses on behalf of HMRC. A taxable person is one who is or should be registered for VAT, because they make taxable supplies A taxable supply is everything which is not exempt or outside the scope of VAT. It includes sales and purchases of most goods or services. ***Input and output VAT*** It is important to distinguish between input and output VAT: - Businesses pay input VAT on their purchases of goods and services. - Input VAT is reclaimable from HMRC. - Registered businesses charge output VAT on their sales of taxable goods and services. - Output VAT is payable to HMRC. - Every month or quarter the input and output VAT is **netted off** and paid to or recovered from HMRC. The business therefore accounts to HMRC for VAT on the 'value added' to the product. # Types of supply Supplies can be taxable, exempt or outside the scope of VAT. ## Taxable supplies VAT is charged on taxable supplies but not on exempt supplies or supplies which are outside the scope of VAT. It is therefore important to be able to correctly classify supplies in order to determine whether VAT should be charged. - It is also important to correctly classify supplies because: - only taxable supplies are taken into account in determining whether a trader needs to register for VAT - input VAT related to exempt supplies is not recoverable. - Taxable supplies are charged to VAT at one of three rates: - **zero rate:** This is a tax rate of nil. No VAT is charged

# C24 — VAT special and overseas issues VAT rules for special or overseas transactions, including place-of-supply and transaction-specific considerations. Original notes: [C24_VAT_OS.qmd](../C24_VAT_OS.qmd) Related: [[C23_VAT]], [[C01_TX_SYS]], [[C12_TX_ADMN]] ## Original note content --- title: "Chapter 24: VAT Overseas Aspects" abstract: | 1. understand how VAT is accounted for and administered.
2. list the information that must be given on a VAT invoice.
3. understand when the penalties for late submission/filing and late payment, and the interest for late payment will be applied.
4. understand the VAT treatment of imports, exports and trade outside the UK.
5. understand postponed accounting for VAT on imports.
6. understand the operation of, and when it will be advantageous to use the VAT special schemes:
- Cash accounting scheme - Annual accounting scheme - Flat rate scheme. --- # VAT: Administration and overseas aspects ## VAT computation All registered traders have to: - complete a VAT return every return period', and - pay net VAT due to HMRC or reclaim net VAT repayable from HMRC. Details of output and input VAT must be included, together with claims for *relief for impairment losses* and *any errors* made on earlier returns below a (***de minimis limit***). #### Example 1: VAT computation Cart Ltd is registered for VAT, and its sales are all **standard-rated**. The following information relates to the company’s VAT return for the quarter ended 31 December 2025: 1. Standard-rated sales amounted to £240,000. 2. In addition to the above Cart Ltd issued a sales invoice for **£25,000** on 1 December 2025. The customer was offered a **5% discount** if the invoice was paid within 14 days. The customer paid within the 14 day period. 3. Standard-rated *purchases and expenses* amounted to **£71,280**. This *figure includes £960 for entertaining UK customers*. 4. On 15 December 2025, the company wrote off **irrecoverable debts** of £4,000 and £1,680, in respect of invoices due for payment on 10 May and 5 August 2025 respectively. ---> Only accept 6m prior 5. On 30 December 2025, the company purchased a car at a cost of £32,900, for the use of a director, and machinery at a cost of £42,300. Both these figures are **inclusive of VAT**. The car is used for both business and private mileage. Unless stated otherwise, all of the above figures are exclusive of VAT. ***Calculate the amount of VAT payable by Cart Ltd for the quarter.*** **Solution** | ***Output VAT*** | £ | |---------------------------------------------------------------|----------| | Sales (£240,000 × 20%) | 48,000 | | Discounted sale (£25,000 × 95% × 20%) | 4,750 | | **Total output VAT** |**52,7

nodes.name: Employment income
nodes.summary: Remuneration and taxable benefits arising from employment, considered alongside employment-related expenses.

nodes.name: National Insurance contributions
nodes.summary: Contributions whose categories and liabilities interact with employment and self-employment income.

nodes.name: Self-employment income
nodes.summary: Trading income of self-employed individuals is a context in which National Insurance liability is considered.

nodes.name: Individual tax administration
nodes.summary: Administrative lifecycle covering registration, returns, deadlines, payment, records, enquiries, penalties, and appeals for individuals.

nodes.name: Corporation-tax computation
nodes.summary: Computation of a company's taxable total profits, rates, reliefs, and payment considerations.

nodes.name: Company loss relief
nodes.summary: Relief mechanisms for company losses against profits across periods or in a corporate group context.

nodes.name: Corporate group
nodes.summary: A group relationship used to analyze loss relief, asset transfers, and planning constraints between companies.

nodes.name: Corporate tax administration
nodes.summary: Company filing, payment, compliance, enquiry, and penalty processes.

nodes.name: Capital-gains framework
nodes.summary: General structure for disposals, gains and losses, allowable costs, annual exemptions, rates, and computations.

nodes.name: Special capital-gains treatment
nodes.summary: Rules for transactions or assets requiring treatment different from the standard capital-gains disposal computation.

nodes.name: NIC connects income categories to individual liability computations
nodes.summary: National Insurance is analyzed in relation to employment and self-employment income and to the wider calculation of individual tax liabilities.

nodes.name: Individual tax administration is a process chain
nodes.summary: The individual administration article groups registration, filing, deadlines, payment, record keeping, enquiries, penalties, and appeals into one compliance lifecycle.

nodes.name: Corporation tax is the corporate computation hub
nodes.summary: The corporation-tax computation provides the central connection between taxable profits, company losses, groups, corporate administration, corporate gains, and VAT context.

nodes.name: Company losses can operate across periods and group context
nodes.summary: Company loss rules address relief against profits across periods and also interact with the corporate-group context.

nodes.name: Group taxation links relief, asset transfers, and planning constraints
nodes.summary: The group-taxation topic combines group relationships with loss relief, asset transfers, and constraints on planning.

nodes.name: Corporate administration operationalizes corporation tax
nodes.summary: Company filing, payment, compliance, enquiry, and penalty rules provide the administrative counterpart to corporation-tax computation.

nodes.name: The standard CGT framework precedes special cases
nodes.summary: The general capital-gains framework supplies the baseline for handling special transactions or assets that require different treatment.

nodes.name: Special CGT cases interact with shares and reliefs
nodes.summary: Special capital-gains cases are positioned alongside share disposals and reorganisations and capital-gains reliefs rather than as an isolated computation.

nodes.name: Share identification and pooling rules
nodes.summary: Same-day, 30-day matching and share-pool rules identify securities disposed of by individuals; companies apply a related but distinct matching framework.

nodes.name: Qualifying corporate bond
nodes.summary: A qualifying corporate bond is a sterling commercial loan instrument meeting the relevant currency, conversion and issue-date conditions and is exempt from individual CGT.

nodes.name: Private residence relief
nodes.summary: Relief for qualifying gains on a dwelling that has been the individual's only or main residence, including eligible actual and deemed occupation periods.

nodes.name: Business asset disposal relief
nodes.summary: An individual capital-gains relief associated with qualifying business disposals and subject to specific ownership, business and eligibility conditions.

nodes.name: Rollover relief
nodes.summary: A capital-gains relief that can defer a gain when qualifying business assets are replaced by qualifying replacement assets.

nodes.name: Corporate chargeable gains
nodes.summary: Company gains and allowable losses are calculated for the accounting period and incorporated into taxable total profits for corporation tax purposes.

nodes.name: Inheritance-tax transfer of value
nodes.summary: A gratuitous disposition that reduces the donor's estate, potentially creating inheritance-tax consequences during lifetime or on death.

nodes.name: Input and output VAT accounting
nodes.summary: Registered businesses offset recoverable input VAT on purchases against output VAT charged on taxable supplies and settle the net amount with HMRC.

nodes.name: VAT place of supply
nodes.summary: The place-of-supply rules determine the VAT treatment of imports, exports and supplies involving locations outside the UK.

nodes.name: VAT special schemes
nodes.summary: Cash accounting, annual accounting and flat-rate schemes provide alternative VAT administration or calculation methods for eligible businesses.

nodes.name: Taxpayer-and-tax classification
nodes.summary: The first step in a mixed tax question is to identify the taxpayer and the relevant tax before classifying the income, asset or transaction.

nodes.name: Tax computation workflow
nodes.summary: A repeatable exam workflow links classification, exemptions or reliefs, liability computation, administration and filing or payment deadlines.

nodes.name: Individual share disposals require ordered matching rules
nodes.summary: For an individual's share disposal, same-day and 30-day matching rules are applied before the relevant share pool is used to determine the allowable cost.

nodes.name: Company gains enter corporation-tax profits
nodes.summary: Companies pay corporation tax on chargeable gains rather than individual CGT; net gains after allowable losses are included in taxable total profits and there is no annual exempt amount.

nodes.name: Capital-gains reliefs alter the amount or timing of tax
nodes.summary: Capital-gains reliefs can exempt part of a gain, reduce the rate or amount payable, or defer the gain; eligibility and interaction conditions must be checked.

nodes.name: Inheritance tax applies to lifetime and death transfers
nodes.summary: The inheritance-tax framework covers death estates as well as specified lifetime transfers, including gifts that become chargeable within the relevant period and transfers into trusts.

nodes.name: VAT liability is a net input-output settlement
nodes.summary: A registered trader's VAT return generally compares output VAT on taxable supplies with recoverable input VAT and reports the resulting amount payable or repayable.

nodes.name: VAT classification drives registration and recovery
nodes.summary: Whether a supply is taxable, exempt or outside scope affects VAT registration calculations and whether related input VAT can be recovered.

nodes.name: Exam questions integrate computation with administration
nodes.summary: Strong exam answers connect taxpayer and transaction classification to computation, reliefs or exemptions, and the applicable filing, payment and deadline rules.
